t: Expeditions map making, for people who have never done it
s: A plain-language guide to building custom maps for Expeditions: A MudRunner Game. Start with a map that loads, then make it good.
x: Make a map for Expeditions # Saber shipped a map editor with the game and a set of official guides to go with it. The guides are accurate. They are also written field by field, in the order the software stores things, which means you can read four pages about deploy zones and still not know what a deploy zone is for. This guide is the other way round. It explains what a thing is and what it is for , then tells you which fields to fill in. It assumes you have never opened the editor. Read this first if you read nothing else # Two rules save more time than everything else on this site combined. Get a map that loads before you make it pretty. A map needs a shape, one deploy zone and one expedition. That is it. Build that on your first day, pack it, and drive around an empty landscape. Now you have a foundation. People who spend three weeks sculpting a canyon and then try to make it load spend the next three weeks finding out why it does not. Your map exists in three places at once , and they drift apart from each other constantly. Almost every “I fixed it and nothing changed” story comes from editing the wrong copy. Read that page early . Where to start # What you need The editor, the folders, and roughly how long things take. Where everything lives Three copies of your map, and which one to edit. x: Your map is not one thing in one folder. It exists in three places, they hold different data, and they fall out of step with each other constantly. Almost every “I fixed it and nothing changed” story ends here. So does almost every “it worked yesterday”. Learn this page and you will skip a category of problem entirely. The three copies # All three live under Documents\My Games\Expeditions\Media\ . Folder What it is Who writes it Who reads it prebuild\<level>\ The source. Your real work lives here The editor, when you save The editor, when you open the map levels\<Level>\ The staging copy. What the zone settings tool shows you, and what the packer reads The editor and the zone tool The packer Mods\<Level>.pak The product. A zip archive The packer The game Read that last column again. s: The shortest path from nothing to driving around your own terrain. Do this before you make anything look good.
x: A playable Expeditions map needs exactly two things: one expedition one deploy zone That is the entire requirement. documented Not a mission, not an objective, not a reward. And the expedition is allowed to be a Free Roam one, which is the simplest possible kind. So the smallest map that works is “here is some ground, drive on it” . Build that first. It proves the whole chain works, from editor to pack to deploy, before you invest real time in anything. Why this order matters # Packing takes about 25 minutes. If you sculpt for a week and only then try to load the map, every problem you find costs half an hour to test a fix for, and you will have several problems, and you will not know which of a week’s changes caused any of them. Get to “I can drive on it” on day one. Then every later problem has a short list of suspects: whatever you did since it last worked. The five steps # 1 ### Make the map and give it a shape Create a new map in the editor and raise some terrain. Do not make it good. A lumpy field is fine. You want geometry that exists, not geometry you like, because you are testing the pipeline and you will probably throw this away. 2 ### Place a deploy zone In the map editor, place a zone object where you want trucks to arrive, and give it an **Id**. Pick a name without spaces or punctuation, something like `main_deploy`. Note it exactly, because the next step has to match it character for character. Put it on reasonably flat ground, and sit it slightly **above** the terrain surface rather than exactly on it. documented Zones that intersect the ground cause collision problems for arriving trucks. 3 **A deploy zone placed on a real-terrain map.** The pink marker is the zone, and the Scene View lists it under Zones as `deploy`. ![A deploy zone placed in the editor

s: Heightmaps, the tile system, and why editing the file you think is the terrain often changes nothing.
x: Terrain in Expeditions is a grid of heights. The editor turns that grid into the ground you drive on. That part is simple. What catches people out is which copy of the grid the editor actually reads, when it reads it, and how precisely a height can be stored at all. This page covers those three things. Get them wrong and you can spend a day editing a file the editor never looks at. Size and height are fixed when you create the map # A map is measured in blocks . Each block is 24 m square. documented You set the number of blocks and the Max height when you create the terrain, and both are read-only in the terrain properties afterwards. setting value block size 24 m maximum blocks per axis 84 , so a full-size map is 2016 m square minimum recommended 5 x 5 blocks, because the edges carry an invisible wall drone no-fly zone 150 m from the edge by default, so very small maps are a poor fit The level name must start with level_ . documented Choose Max height with care, because you cannot change it later. A value of 512 has been used on maps that load and drive in game. measured Whether values above 512 work has not been tested. Where the heights live # A map keeps its height in more than one place. Only one of them is what the editor builds from. Media\prebuild\<map>.xml descriptor: blocks, Max height, materials Media\prebuild\<map>\_height_source.png a height image you can import (see below) Media\prebuild\<map>\data\<col>_<row>\ 16 TILES, each with its own _height.dds Media\levels\<map>\height_map.dds the BUILT result Every map is split into 16 pieces , 0_0 to 3_3 , whatever its size. documented Each piece has a folder under data\ holding that piece’s height, masks and blends. s: Size, falloff and strength, and why a soft brush where a hard one belongs turns a road into a row of domes.
x: A brush is how you change the ground by hand in the editor. You pick one in the Scene View, set three numbers, and paint. Almost every brush in the editor works the same way, so learning one teaches you most of them. How painting works # Select a brush by selecting its node in the Scene View. The Geometry node and its sub-nodes are the terrain brushes. documented Hold the right mouse button and move to paint. Click the left mouse button to apply what you painted. Undo Current Changes in the brush dialog throws away everything since your last right-click. Then rebuild to see the result: right-click the scene and choose Rebuild Terrain, or Rebuild visible / Selection for part of it. The toolbar’s Enable autorebuild terrain rebuilds each time you switch brushes. documented The three controls # Every brush has the same three controls. documented control what it does Size the brush’s size, in metres Value how hard each pass pushes, and in which direction. Negative values are allowed: on the height brush, positive raises and negative digs Falloff how soft the brush’s edge is. 0 is a completely hard edge. 1 starts fading straight from the centre Two more appear on many brushes: Autofade weakens the stroke depending on the direction you draw. Saber suggests it for ruts and mud. Randomize varies the strength randomly within a range, for rough, chaotic ground. Some brushes do nothing at their default value On brushes whose Value runs from 0 to 1 , a value above 0.50 paints and a value below 0.50 removes. The default is usually 0.50 , which does nothing until you move it. documented Falloff is the control that matters most # Falloff 0 is a hard brush. It changes the whole circle by the same amount, so it leaves a flat top with steep sides. That is what you want for a bench, a wall

s: Roads are Overlay objects laid on top of the ground, and two of the defaults are backwards for a usable road.
x: This is the biggest single time sink for a new map maker: sculpting roads into the heightmap by hand when the editor has a road tool. A road in Expeditions is an Overlay : a curve you draw across the map, carrying a road surface that drapes over the ground underneath. documented The same tool lays railway track, pipes and wires. You do not dig a road. You lay one, and then decide how much it should reshape the ground it sits on. Expeditions is an off-road game, and Saber notes that ordinary road overlays are used much less here than in SnowRunner. The game does ship Expeditions-specific ones such as animal_tracks , cracked_mud and log_road . documented Digging roads by hand goes badly Excavating a road into the heightmap produced a bare scar on a sidehill. Forcing a drivable gradient across 150 m of relief moved 30 m of earth, which leaves a cliff wherever the cut meets untouched ground. measured Laying an overlay # Right-click the terrain, or the Overlays node in the Scene View, and choose Add Overlay . Double-click a road type in the window that opens. The overlay appears with two points, numbered from 0 . To add points, select one, right-click it and choose Add after or Add before . Move a point with the arrows, or type its Position X and Position Y . Set the width at each point: drag sideways from the point’s centre, or type a Width . Rebuild Terrain to see the final result. Parts of an overlay outside the camera’s view may not update until you do. documented The toolbar’s Hide all nodes of rivers and overlays hides the red point markers when they get in the way. Keep Change rotation basis off while you work on points: Saber warns that it blocks selecting individual overlay points. documented What an overlay is on disk # The editor saves each overlay as its own file

s: Give water somewhere to go, hide the edges, and keep the result editable whether you build it yourself or with AI.
x: A river is not a blue road. Putting a strip of water across a valley does not make that strip fit the valley. It gives you a water surface. The ground still has to provide the bed and the banks. Get those three things to agree first. Foam can wait. What a water object is # All water in a map, flowing or still, is a River object. documented It is a line of points, like a road overlay , with one important difference: every point has a height , and that height is the level of the water surface there. A River is a surface, not a channel. It lays water over whatever is beneath it. It does not cut a bed. Saber’s own order of work starts with “prepare a deepening of the terrain” before you add any water. documented On disk a point looks like this: measured <River Flow= "0" NeedFlowMapLoading= "false" Clean= "emerald" Muddy= "brown" ... > <Node Position= "(x; y; z)" Width= "16.17662" /> </River> The middle number, y , is the water height. Unlike an overlay, the points are direct children of <River> , with no <Curve> around them. The settings that matter # setting what it does UseFlowMap false : water flows from point 0 towards the last point. true : you paint the direction with the Water brush AvoidEffectOpacity false (default): shallow water runs slower and with smaller waves. true : shallow but wild, for mountain streams Clean Type the water’s colour where it is clean Muddy Type the colour where you paint it muddy with the WaterMud brush AboveReferences keeps this river’s colours from being overridden by imported references documented To reverse a river’s flow, right-click it in the Scene View and choose River … Invert . documented In the saved file, UseFlowMap appears as NeedFlowMapLoading . measured The colour types are classes in the game files, such as emerald , emerald_d

s: Importing real elevation data, and the surprising amount of design work it does for you.
x: You do not have to invent your landscape. Public survey data gives you the height of real ground, and a real place has already solved problems that are hard to solve by hand: where the valleys drain, how steep the slopes sit, and where a road can climb a hillside. This page covers where that data comes from, what it does and does not contain, and the checks that catch the mistakes it makes easy. Where the data comes from # source coverage resolution notes USGS 3DEP United States 1 m bare-earth lidar, no API key. Best by far global terrain tiles (AWS terrarium set) worldwide roughly 10 to 30 m too coarse for roads to show up measured Bare-earth means the survey has had trees and buildings removed, leaving the ground itself. At 1 m that is finer than the map’s own height grid, which on a full-size map is 0.5 m per sample in the built terrain and 2 m per sample in the import file. The 3DEP service refuses very large requests, so a full map is fetched in pieces of about 2000 pixels each and stitched. measured Fetching it with the toolkit # fetch_terrain.py fetches 3DEP for a point, crops it to the map’s size and writes the import file at the size the editor expects. It also reports the Max height to use and the height step that results. python fetch_terrain.py <lat> <lon> --span 2016 --blocks 84 python fetch_terrain.py <lat> <lon> --span 2016 --blocks 84 --level level_<name> --apply Then open the map in the editor and use Copy Source Heightmap to import it. Read how terrain works first: the import replaces the whole terrain, and a baked terrain file left from a copied map will hide the result. Outside the United States the toolkit’s expeditions/dem.py uses the global tiles instead. That route has not been tested on a map in this guide. A real heightmap straight after import

s: Terrain texture layers, tint maps, and getting the colour of a real place right.
x: The colour of a map comes from three separate systems, and it helps to know which one you are looking at before trying to change it: What you see Where it comes from Painted with the ground’s texture: sand, gravel, grass, rock PBR materials and their layers the PbrMaterials brush a colour cast over that texture tint the Colorization brush roads and tracks overlays , which carry their own texture the Overlay tool Water colour is a fourth, set per river. See Rivers, lakes and waterfalls . How much of this is tested Materials, layers, the Colorization brush and the overlay limit are from Saber’s guides. The tint file layout and the colour derivation come from work on a real map. Custom ground textures have been worked out from the shipped files but not built as a finished workflow, and are labelled. Terrain texture layers # Ground textures are painted with PBR materials . documented Right-click the terrain (or the PbrMaterials section of the Scene View) and choose Add PbrMaterial . Each material has 4 layers , and a map can have at most 4 materials . Each layer is a texture: sand, gravel, rock, grass and so on. Two levels of painting # This is the part that is easy to miss. documented Opacity mode paints which material a terrain block uses. It works per 24 m block, and each block can use one material only. Then the layer modes paint that material’s layers within the blocks. With more than one material, do the Opacity painting first. Because a block holds one material, the boundary between two materials falls on a block edge and can show as a hard line. Saber’s fix: use the same textures as layers on both sides of a boundary, so the blocks blend across it. As with the other brushes, holding the right mouse button paints; a Value above 0.50 adds the layer and below 0.50 eras

s: Background music is a table keyed by level name and can be added to a map that is already packed. Ambient sound cannot. How to tell which one you are holding, and the two pak members that decide whether anyone but you hears it.
x: Music and sound # Music and ambient sound look like one feature and behave like two. Music is a lookup table the game reads at runtime. Ambient sound is part of the scene. That difference decides how much work a change costs, so it is worth being able to tell them apart before you start. The test # pak.load_list inside a packed map is the engine’s index of that level’s resources. Count what appears in it. On a shipped map that plays four music tracks and has an ambient eagle call: references to 'eagle' 28 references to 'magic_whispers' 0 references to 'music_presets' 0 The ambient sound is indexed. The music is not. in the index in the scene needs the editor music no no no ambient or positional sound yes yes yes So music can be added to a map that is already finished and packed. An ambient sound has a position, which means opening the map, placing it, saving, repacking, and getting it into the index. s: A zone is a shape in the world plus a set of properties, and those two halves live in two different programs.
x: Read this before the other zone pages. A zone is two things that get edited separately, and once you see the split, most zone problems explain themselves. s: Fog of war, and the setting that will accidentally hide a zone you wanted available.
x: Most zone props carry a zoneDiscoverability block. It decides whether the player can see the zone when the expedition starts, and if not, how they get to find it: by driving there, by flying a drone over it, or by spotting it through binoculars. Used on purpose it is one of the best tools a map has, because finding things is the point of an expedition. Used by accident, it hides a zone you meant to be open and gives you no hint why. What on this page has been tested That a zone with no discoverability block is simply available is proven: deploy zones set up that way on working maps load and deploy. The rest is from Saber’s guides and from the settings in working maps. It has not been tested state by state in game, and the specialist requirements and discovery rewards are untested. Leave it empty unless you mean it # A zone with no discoverability settings is simply available. Its marker is there from the start, and nothing has to be found. This is the right answer far more often than people expect: a deploy zone, a store, a delivery target the briefing already tells the player about. In Zone Settings an unused block is null . On the working maps this guide was built from, every main deploy zone has it null . s: How you order a mission. Stages run in sequence, the assignments inside one stage run in any order, and that is the whole mechanic.
x: This is the one concept the official guides bury, and once you have it the rest of the mission system is just filling in fields. Two rules # An objective is a list of stages . Each stage contains one or more assignments , which the software calls substages . Stages run in order. Stage 0, then stage 1, then stage 2. Assignments inside one stage run in any order , and all must finish before that stage closes. That is it. There is no scripting, no triggers, no conditions, no branching. What that looks like # Say you want the player to reach a ridge, grab a winch anchor, then bridge a wash, then tow a wreck home. s: Every kind of job you can give a player, what each one needs, and the three that exist in the engine but not in the official guides.
x: An assignment is one thing you ask the player to do. A stage holds one or more of them. There are eleven kinds, and the official guides document eight . The eight documented kinds # visitAllZones # Reach one or more places. The simplest assignment and the one you will use most. Each target can optionally be reached by drone instead of by truck, or by drone only . Drone-only needs two settings, not one To require the drone you must turn on both visitWithDroneOnly and mayVisitZoneWithDrone . With only the first, trucks are forbidden and drones were never allowed, so the zone becomes unreachable by any means. documented Also: the default drone cannot fly within 170 m of the map edge, and cannot climb more than 30 m above the truck. A drone-only target outside those limits is impossible. documented takeInventory # Collect specific items from specific places. You name the item type, optionally a specific item id, and how many. Works with custom items. If you have made your own device, its id goes here like any other. objectConstruction # Deliver something to a place. That something can be an inventory item, fuel , repair parts , or any combination. At least one of the three must be set or there is nothing to deliver. The name comes from what it is usually used for: tying the delivery to a model that appears once the goods arrive, which is how bridges get built. That part is optional, and the delivery works fine without it. Two useful extras: additionalUnloadZones lets the goods be delivered to an alternative place. The base game uses this for bridges buildable from either bank. modelPlacementZones blocks the delivery while a truck is parked somewhere it would be clipped by the model appearing. truckDelivery # Drive a truck that is already placed on the map to a destination.

s: SnowRunner and Expeditions share the mod format, so a SnowRunner vehicle's meshes load untouched. Its textures do not, and that is why ported trucks come out solid black.
x: Porting a SnowRunner truck # Doing a port? Start with the runbook. Porting runbook, start to finish is the ordered procedure with every trap at the step where it bites. This page explains why the big one happens, and is worth reading once. Expeditions and SnowRunner are both Saber engine games and they share one mod format. Saber’s own documentation covers truck modding for both titles in a single section, which tells you how close they are. So a SnowRunner vehicle mod can be brought into Expeditions. People already do it — BFW, iX-5 and ULM C10 are community ports. But there is one asymmetry that costs most people their first attempt, and it is worth understanding before you start. The one thing that breaks # Meshes port untouched. Textures do not. A published mod contains compiled geometry and converted textures. The geometry is cross-compatible: drop a SnowRunner truck into Expeditions and it will spawn, drive, steer and articulate its suspension perfectly. Its textures will not load, and the vehicle renders solid black — body, glass, wheels, everything. A ported SnowRunner pickup in a running game, before re-encoding. It drives, but every surface is black. The log says: Failed to load texture textures/<modid>\trucks/carroceria__d_a.tga The reason is that the mod’s .pct textures were encoded by SnowRunner’s converter, and Expeditions cannot decode them. When a texture fails, the engine falls back to looking for the source .tga , which a packed mod never ships. So every material on the vehicle ends up with no albedo at all. measured The .pct container header is byte-identical between the two games: magic TCIP , version 258, header size 32, same width and height fields. You cannot tell a SnowRunner texture from an Expeditions one by looking at it. The truck going black

s: A colour preset does not only carry three colours — it names a material override, which can replace the albedo outright. That is how you get a wrap, chrome or camouflage instead of a repaint.
x: Skins and paint # A CustomizationPreset is the button the player presses in the garage. It looks like it carries three tint colours, and it does, but it also names a MaterialOverride — and an override can replace the albedo outright. That is the difference between offering a repaint and offering a livery. <MaterialOverride AlbedoMap= "trucks/carroceria_jungle__d.tga" Name= "skin_jungle" TargetMaterialName= "carroceria" TintMap= "trucks/carroceria_notint__d.tga" /> <CustomizationPreset Id= "14" MaterialOverrideName= "skin_jungle" TintColor1= "..." /> The two rules that make it work properly # Give a pattern a tint mask with R=0 # The red channel of the TintMap defines the overall paint zone, so an area with no red never tints . A camouflage or livery then shows exactly as painted instead of being recoloured by whatever the preset’s tint happens to be. The same mechanism pins a part to a fixed colour. A hard top that should always be black gets a black albedo and an R=0 mask, and the garage colour picker then cannot touch it while still recolouring the body around it. Mirror the override onto every mesh that has the others # Addons, bumpers and racks carry their own MaterialOverride entries. Add a new skin only to the body and the body goes camouflage while the bumpers stay factory. The practical rule: for each mesh, find the materials skin_00 already targets, and add the new skin for the same ones. Packing is the step that turns the map you edit into the files the game loads, and the same is true of a custom module, specialist or item. The flow runs one way. You edit the source, you pack, the game reads the pak. Nothing in the pak flows back into your source, so a fix made only in the pak is lost the next time you pack. x: Lessons that transfer to other games # Nothing in the formats carries over.
